# Results — Study 30 (House-Edge) on the real S&P 500

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily S&P 500 total-return proxy (`^GSPC`,
auto-adjusted) and the 13-week T-bill (`^IRX`) as the financing rate, 1990–2026. The strategy is a
vol-targeted contrarian dip-buyer (RSI(2) entries, `target_vol/realised_vol` sizing, 200-day trend gate)
run under two cost models — **idealized** (finance only the slice above 100%, no dividends) and **honest**
(full notional financed at T-bill + 2.5% markup, dividends credited, idle cash earning the bill). The
offline core proves the machinery on a synthetic GARCH-with-bear-regimes index; this is the measurement on
the market. As-of **2026-06-09**; match the fingerprint below.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · Free leverage? `Busted`

The risk management is real and the return edge is a mirage. The vol-targeted, trend-gated book **halves
the worst drawdown** — **−27.8%** versus buy-and-hold's **−55.7%** — exactly what a vol-targeting overlay
is supposed to do, and it holds on the synthetic control too (**−35%** vs **−44%**). But once leverage is
financed *honestly* — the whole notional, every day, the way a CFD or margin account actually funds — the
strategy earns a CAGR of **5.3%** against the total-return index's **10.6%**: **half the return**, at a
*lower* Sharpe (**0.42** vs **0.65**) and an **identical Calmar (0.19)**. It does not beat buy-and-hold at
*any* financing markup we try. The thing you actually buy is drawdown insurance, paid for one-for-one in
forgone return — not a market-beating edge.

| Strategy — **honest** costs | **5.3%** | **0.42** | **−27.8%** | 0.19 |

## The house edge — what the optimistic accounting hides

Same exposure path, two cost models: **idealized 6.8% − honest 5.3% = 1.55 pts/yr**. Average exposure
**0.97×**. That 1.55%/yr is the broker's house edge on your leverage — the financing the "finance only the
excess over 100%, ignore dividends" convention leaves off, and the reason a levered-timing backtest looks
better on a slide than in an account.

## It never beats buy-and-hold — the financing-markup sweep

Honest strategy vs the total-return hold, as the broker markup over the T-bill rises:

| markup over T-bill | strategy CAGR | strategy Sharpe | edge vs buy & hold (CAGR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0% | 7.9% | 0.59 | **−2.7%** |
| 1.0% | 6.8% | 0.52 | **−3.8%** |
| 2.5% | 5.3% | 0.42 | **−5.3%** |
| 5.0% | 2.8% | 0.26 | **−7.9%** |

Negative at every financing cost — even at a zero markup (funding at the pure bill rate), the levered book
still trails the index it is levering. Not a tuning miss: the return shortfall is structural.

## The part that is real — drawdown protection

| | strategy | buy & hold |
|---|---|---|
| max-drawdown | **−27.8%** | −55.7% |
| Calmar | 0.19 | 0.19 |

The drawdown is halved (a **27.8-point** reduction) — genuine, robust risk control. But the Calmar tie is
the whole story in one number: per unit of drawdown survived, the strategy and the plain index pay the
same. You can buy a smoother ride; you cannot, this way, buy a bigger one. Signal `REAL`, Tradability
`MIRAGE`, free leverage? `Busted`.
